title: How passwords actually get stolen — and the 4 habits that stop it
description: Hardly anyone has their password guessed by a hacker typing in a dark room. Passwords get tricked out of people with fake login pages, leaked in data breaches and reused elsewhere, copied by infostealer malware, or cracked because they're short and common. This video walks through all four routes, with real figures from Verizon, the UK government, the NCSC and NIST, and finishes with four habits that shut each one down, plus a 10-minute action plan.

scenes.sub: they get it a smarter way
scenes.say: When people imagine a hacker stealing a password, they picture someone in a dark room, guessing over and over until something works. That almost never happens. Most stolen passwords are tricked out of people, bought from someone who already has them, or scooped up by malware. In this video you'll see the four main ways it happens, and the four habits that shut each one down.

scenes.title: How breaches start
scenes.say: Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report looked at thousands of real breaches. The most common way in was credential abuse: attackers simply logging in with a username and password that wasn't theirs. That narrowly beat exploiting software vulnerabilities. So in a huge share of breaches, nobody broke in at all. They used a key.

Here are the four routes we'll cover. One: fake login pages. Two: data breaches, and the password reuse that makes them so dangerous. Three: malware that quietly copies your saved logins. And four: guessing, which only really works on weak passwords. Let's take them one at a time.

scenes.sub: of UK businesses with a breach said phishing was involved
scenes.say: Phishing is still the biggest problem. In the UK government's Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025, eighty-five per cent of businesses that identified a breach or attack said phishing was involved. It's cheap, it scales, and it catches clever people too.

scenes.caption: A fake login page
scenes.say: A phishing message usually creates panic: your account is locked, a parcel is stuck, a payment failed. The link leads to a page that looks exactly like the real login screen, on an address that's slightly off, like PayPal spelt with a number one. Whatever you type goes straight to the attacker.

The defence isn't spotting every fake, because some are very good. It's a habit: never log in from a link in a message. Open the app, or type the address yourself. And a bonus: password managers only fill in your password on the real site, so if yours refuses to autofill, treat that as a big red flag.

scenes.question: Your bank texts a link saying your account is locked. What do you do?
scenes.say: Quick check. Your bank texts you a link saying your account is locked. What do you do? The answer: ignore the link, and open the bank's own app, or ring the number on the back of your card. If there's a real problem, you'll see it there.

scenes.sub: breached accounts listed on Have I Been Pwned
scenes.say: Websites get breached all the time. The free service Have I Been Pwned now lists almost eighteen billion breached accounts, from more than a thousand hacked websites. If you've been online for a few years, your email address is very likely in there somewhere.

steps: Bots try them on other sites
scenes.say: On its own, one breach is bad. The real damage comes from reuse. Attackers take the leaked email and password pairs and feed them to bots that try them on banks, shops, email and social media. This is called credential stuffing. If you used the same password anywhere else, they're in, without guessing a thing.

scenes.caption: Logins tried by the thousand
scenes.say: From the website's side, it looks like this: thousands of logins, each with a different real email address. Most fail. A few succeed. Those few are people who reused a password. The site itself might be perfectly secure. The weak point was a breach somewhere else, maybe years ago.

scenes.sub: so a breach stays in one place
scenes.say: That's why a different password for every account matters so much. A breach then only exposes that one site, and the stolen password is useless everywhere else.

The third route is malware called an infostealer. It usually arrives disguised as something you wanted: cracked software, free game cheats or mods, a fake download page found through a search ad, or an attachment in a phishing email. The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists all of these as common ways in.

scenes.caption: What infostealers grab
scenes.say: Once it runs, it works fast. It copies passwords saved in your browser, the session cookies that keep you logged in, autofill data like card details, and crypto wallets. Then it sends the lot to the attacker, who often sells it on. Stolen session cookies can even let them skip your password and two-step check, by reusing a session you've already logged into.

The defence is mostly about what you install. Get apps and games from official stores and developers. Keep automatic updates on, so known holes get patched. Leave your built-in protection, like Microsoft Defender, switched on. And if you ever do run something dodgy, change your passwords from a different, clean device, and sign out of every session.

scenes.title: Most hacked passwords
scenes.say: Guessing does happen, but mostly against weak passwords. When the UK's National Cyber Security Centre analysed breached accounts, one two three four five six turned up more than twenty-three million times. Next came one to nine, qwerty, password, and a row of ones. Attackers try these first, because they work.

scenes.caption: Weak passwords fall first
scenes.say: When a site is breached, attackers often get scrambled versions of the passwords, called hashes. They can't simply reverse them, but they can make enormous numbers of guesses offline, starting with leaked password lists and predictable tweaks, like a capital letter and a year. Short or common passwords fall quickly. Long, random ones hold out.

scenes.sub: NIST's minimum for a password used on its own
scenes.say: Length is what beats guessing. The US standards body NIST now says a password used on its own should be at least fifteen characters, and that sites shouldn't force odd symbol rules or regular changes. The UK's NCSC suggests three random words. Long, random, and still easy to remember.

steps: Never log in from a message link
scenes.say: So here are the four habits, and each one shuts a door. One: use a password manager, with a unique password for every account. Two: turn on two-step verification, or better still, passkeys. Three: never log in from a link in a message. Four: only install software from official sources, and keep updates on.

scenes.sub: lower risk of account compromise with MFA (Microsoft study)
scenes.say: Habit two deserves a number. A Microsoft research study of real accounts found that multi-factor authentication cut the risk of compromise by more than ninety-nine per cent, and by over ninety-eight per cent even when the password had already leaked. A stolen password on its own stops being enough.

items: Can be typed into a fake
Can be phished in real time

right.label: Passkey
items: Only works on the real site
Nothing to type or hand over

scenes.say: Passkeys go a step further. A one-time code can still be typed into a convincing fake page. A passkey can't, because your device checks the website's real address, and the passkey only works on the site it was made for. There's nothing to type, so there's nothing to hand over. If an account offers passkeys, turn them on.

scenes.question: Which best protects you from a fake login page?
scenes.say: Quick quiz. Which of these best protects you from a fake login page? A longer password, a passkey, or changing your password every month? It's the passkey. A long password still works if you type it into the wrong site, and forced monthly changes just lead to predictable passwords.

Here's a ten-minute plan. First, check your email address on Have I Been Pwned. Then set up a password manager, either the one built into your phone or browser, or a standalone one. Next, turn on two-step verification for your email, because email is the key that resets everything else. Then add a passkey anywhere it's offered.

scenes.sub: you don't have to be an expert
scenes.say: Over the next few weeks, change any reused passwords, starting with email, banking and shopping. You don't need to be an expert. You just need to stop being the easy target. If this helped, subscribe to Plain Text Threats, and share it with someone who still uses the same password everywhere.
